I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

I should have protected others and I failed

issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: At forty, Tariq sat in the crew lounge of the central ambulance station, the familiar hum of the bay surrounding him. His younger brother Samir had been in a multi-vehicle collision on a rain-slicked highway, and Tariq was the one who pulled him from the wreckage. Samir's temple bore a deep, splitting laceration, blood dark against his skin, and the arriving medical teams carried equipment that released a sharp antiseptic sting. Tariq had tried to steady Samir's shoulder, but his hands felt clumsy, his grip uncertain. He remembered the terror rising in his throat, identical to the moment Samir's breath hitched, though the precise seconds of the impact simply vanished from his mind. He would carry forward a permanent sense that he had shifted, that something fundamental in him had broken. In the weeks that followed, Tariq's days became a study in quiet recalibration. The hospital antiseptic smell, once routine, now drew him sharply back to the triage room. He found himself stepping back when the scent wafted from the station. Visual reminders appeared without warning: a colleague's bandaged wrist, a patient's scraped knee, and each one would pull the memory of Samir's split temple into sharp focus. He would suppress the intrusion, trying hard not to think about the wreckage, redirecting his attention to charts and the steady rhythm of the bay. Yet the fear remained. He would react with alarm when a partner clapped him on the back unexpectedly, his shoulders tightening as though bracing for impact. When he remembered the event, it was not a distant recollection but a full sensory reliving, as though the heat of the engine and the pressure of Samir's cooling arm returned all at once, bringing back the same terror he had felt in the wreckage. He was certain he had failed to protect Samir, that if only he had been closer, the outcome might have been different. What frightened him most was the conviction that he could no longer rely on himself to navigate the bay without hesitation. His occupation, once a source of steady purpose, became a landscape of quiet habits. Tariq began overworking, throwing himself into extracalls and double shifts to keep his mind occupied. His avoidance of the station coexisted with this habit. He started choosing his seat in the crew lounge and the ambulance based on how safe or protected he felt, always preferring the rear corner or the window-facing bench where he could see approaching vehicles and avoid being boxed in. At the station, he would linger near the supply closet, letting younger medics take the front-line patients whose visible injuries mirrored Samir's. His concentration and his radio transmissions shared a fractured rhythm; he would lose his place in handoffs, his thoughts drifting to the gaps in his memory, to the seconds he simply could not recall. The consequences accumulated without drama. His wife, Layla, noticed how he had come to believe the event had permanently altered his temperament, how he flinched when she brushed a strand of hair from his face and how he routinely declined evening calls, citing fatigue rather than fear. His partners observed the shift: the reliable Tariq who once moved swiftly through trauma now paused too long, his gaze fixed on wounds, his breathing measured but taut. His clinical profile rested at a PCL5 of 36, a steady accumulation of symptoms. What finally brought him to the clinic was a routine shift when a young patient bled from a scalp laceration. The antiseptic scent from the triage bay rose around him, the visual trigger sharp, and for a moment, the terror of that evening in the wreckage returned. He stood in the crew lounge, unsure whether to call for backup or step forward, caught between the urge to suppress the memory and the weight of his overworked body. He had come to seek help hoping to understand why the past felt so present, and why, despite everything, he no longer trusted his own hands to hold what mattered.
